title: Geometry of ordinary least squares
dek: OLS is the orthogonal projection of Y onto the column space of X. Residuals are what is left in the orthogonal complement.
story: Write Y ∈ ℝⁿ and X an n×p matrix with full column rank. The OLS fit Ŷ = P_X Y, where P_X = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is the hat matrix, the orthogonal projector onto col(X). β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ Y is the coordinate of that projection in the X basis.

Residuals e = (I − P_X) Y live in the orthogonal complement. That is why Xᵀ e = 0: residuals are uncorrelated with the columns you projected onto, in the sample inner product. Adding a column to X can only shrink ‖e‖, never increase it.

If ε ~ N(0, σ² I), then Ŷ and e are independent, eᵀe / σ² ~ χ²_{n−p}, and the usual t and F tests are exact. The geometry did not need Gaussianity to define the projection; Gaussianity made the sampling laws pretty.
deepTitle: Hat diagonals, collinearity, and the likelihood
deep: Leverage hᵢᵢ = (P_X)ᵢᵢ, between 0 and 1, with ∑ hᵢᵢ = p. A high-leverage isolate is far in covariate space; it can own its fitted value. Geometry first, “outlier” talk second.

Collinearity: if two columns are nearly linearly dependent, col(X) is well defined but the coordinates β̂ are unstable — XᵀX has a large condition number. Predictions Ŷ can still be fine where the design actually sits.

Likelihood: under Y ~ N(Xβ, σ² I), the log-likelihood is −(n/2) log σ² − ‖Y − Xβ‖² / (2σ²). Maximising in β is exactly minimising the residual sum of squares. OLS is MLE in that Gaussian identity GLM, which is why this plate sits under the GLM family tree.

Weighted least squares is the same picture in a different inner product: ⟨u,v⟩_W = uᵀ W v. GLS with known covariance V uses W = V⁻¹. Estimated V (GLS, mixed models) makes the projector random; that is a different sampling story.

formulas.label: OLS projector
formulas.expression: Ŷ = P_X Y,   P_X = X(XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ
formulas.note: P_X² = P_X = P_Xᵀ. Rank p if X has full column rank.

visual.caption: Y is split into a fitted vector in the column space of X and a residual in the orthogonal complement. OLS is that split, not a causal claim about the columns.

example.title: Two-column design, one residual check
example.setup: n = 5 isolates, X = [1, dose], dose = (0,0,1,1,4). Y = log MIC. After OLS, the point with dose 4 has hᵢᵢ large. Geometry says that point owns its fitted value.

steps.title: Rank
steps.body: Two independent columns, p = 2. Residual df = 3. P_X is 5×5 with trace 2.

steps.title: Leverage
steps.body: The dose = 4 row is far from the cloud at 0–1. Its hᵢᵢ will sit well above the mean leverage p/n = 0.4. A small residual there can still be influential once you look at Cook’s distance (diagnostics plate).

steps.title: Likelihood link
steps.body: If you believe Gaussian identity errors, this projection is the MLE. If MIC is censored at an assay ceiling, the likelihood is no longer ‖Y − Xβ‖² and the geometry is only a starting value.

example.takeaway: See the projection first. Coefficients are coordinates; leverage is geometry; Gaussianity is extra.

choices: The orthogonal projector onto the column space of X
check.answer: The orthogonal projector onto the column space of X
check.why: Ŷ = P_X Y is the geometric definition of OLS.

whyWrong.The covariance of β̂: That is σ² (XᵀX)⁻¹ under Gauss–Markov plus spherical errors.
whyWrong.Always equal to I_n: Only if col(X) is all of ℝⁿ, i.e. p = n, perfect fit.

check.prompt: n = 40, p = 5 (full rank, includes intercept). ∑ᵢ hᵢᵢ equals:
check.why: trace(P_X) = rank(P_X) = p = 5. Mean leverage is p/n = 0.125.

whyWrong.40: That is n, trace of I.
whyWrong.1: Trace of a single dummy, not this P.

check.prompt: On the mechanism map, Y splits into col(X) and col(X)⊥. That split is OLS because:
check.figureHint: Project versus residual arrows from Y.
choices: Residuals are chosen to maximise R² by including the complement in the fit
The fitted vector is the closest point of col(X) to Y in Euclidean distance, leaving the residual orthogonal
Causal effects always lie in the complement
check.answer: The fitted vector is the closest point of col(X) to Y in Euclidean distance, leaving the residual orthogonal
check.why: Orthogonal projection is nearest-point geometry. That is OLS.

whyWrong.Residuals are chosen to maximise R² by i: The complement is left out of the fit by construction.
whyWrong.Causal effects always lie in the complem: Causality is not geometry of X.
